title: Health metrics cookbook: latency, uptime, cost/token, cache-hit framework
content:
Purpose:
This is a working cookbook for QBRs and renewal conversations that standardizes how we define and calculate the four core CS metrics we lean on for health and renewal: latency, uptime (availability), cost-per-token, and cache hit rate.

Audience and usage notes:
- Primary readers: CSMs preparing QBR decks, CS Ops building trackers, Solutions Engineers validating dashboards.
- This doc intentionally mixes precise definitions (for engineering/observability) with QBR-friendly phrasing and suggested talking points.
- Open questions and TODOs are flagged with >>>TODO.

1) Latency (customer-facing and engineering variants)
Definition synopsis:
- Customer-facing latency (CF-latency): median and tail user-perceived latency for a full request-response cycle from API recv to last token delivered to the client (includes network, routing, scheduling, decoding). Report p50 / p95 / p99.
- Engineering/slot latency (E-latency): internal service time measured inside serving runtime (time spent on GPU/worker excluding network ingress/egress). Useful for capacity planning.

Measurement specifics:
- Windowing: use rolling 30-day and 7-day windows. For QBRs use 30-day historical plus 7-day trend.
- Aggregation rules: report p50/p95/p99 on completed requests only; exclude canceled/timeout requests but track them separately.
- Sampling: if >100M requests/day, sample at 1% for high-res tails; ensure sample is random and preserves heavy users.
- Token-length normalization: stratify by request length buckets: short (<64 tokens out), medium (64-512), long (>512). Always show p95 per bucket because tails differ hugely by sequence length.

Breakdown categories to show in QBR:
- Network (ingress+egress) median, - Scheduling/queue wait, - Decode/LM generation time (E-latency), - Post-processing (webhook, function calls).
- Visual: stacked bar for p95 showing contributions.

SLO / SLA guidance for QBRs (example targets):
- p50 < 80ms (short), p95 < 180ms (short) for interactive chat models on Dedicated/Hosted.
- p95 budget for medium: <350ms; long: <800ms (depends on model family).
- >>>TODO: formalize per-customer SLOs into renewal contract templates.

QBR talking points (latency):
- "We tracked a 12% improvement in p95 for short requests after enabling bufferless decode in Release X. This decreased tail latency and improved end-user interactivity."
- If degraded: "Tail latency increased due to higher long-request traffic; we recommend applying per-route concurrency limits and autoscale bump for Dedicated."

2) Uptime / Availability
Definition:
- Availability = 1 - (sum of error + failed infra attempts + downstream timeouts) / total requests measured over the chosen window. Expressed as percentage.
- Two flavors: API availability (success HTTP 200-series) and Serving availability (ability to accept and complete requests at the routing layer, excluding client-side failures).

Measurement specifics:
- Windowing: 30-day SLA window. For SLO math use 28-day rolling to align with billing cycles.
- Partial degradations: count minutes of degraded capacity (e.g., 50% of capacity) as proportional downtime for the affected capacity slice.
- Business-hours vs global: For region-based enterprises, compute both global 24/7 availability and region-business-hours availability (customer-specific).

SLA example language for QBRs:
- "Platform availability for last 30 days: 99.93% (SLA target 99.9%). We exceeded the target; incidents impacting availability were mitigated with automatic fallback routing."

Escalation triggers and playbook (customer-facing):
- If availability < SLA - 0.05% for 30d -> CS Ops review -> triage with SRE -> propose remediation plan and UTR (update to renewal risk).
- For persistent repeated partial degradations (3+ in 90 days) -> elevate in renewal discussion as potential commercial credit or Dedicated migration incentive.

3) Cost-per-token (CPT) — how we compute and what to show
Definition and customer phrasing:
- CPT = (Total $ charged for inference window) / (Billable token units). Show separate breakdowns: input tokens, output tokens, embeddings units (if used), and function calls (if priced).

Engineering/calculation notes:
- Billable token counting: follow billing rules (e.g., count raw tokens passed through tokenizer; include both prompt and completion unless customer has special contract).
- Model family multiplier: some models have a cost multiplier (e.g., large-decoder * 1.8) — expose normalized CPT and model-adjusted CPT.
- Discounts & committed usage: for QBRs show "effective CPT" after committed capacity discounts. This is what impacts renewal conversation.
- Caching offsets: show theoretical CPT vs observed CPT after cache savings. E.g., baseline CPT $0.0033/token, observed effective $0.0026/token after 22% cache savings.

Table (example) for QBR slide:
- Time window: last 30 days
- Total billable tokens: 1,245,678,912
- Raw platform cost: $4,115.23
- Effective CPT (post discounts): $0.00330/token
- Cache savings: 21.8% -> effective realized CPT: $0.00258/token
- Action item: Explore further prompt canonicalization to reduce unique prompt fraction by 8-12% (see Optimize playbook).

4) Cache hit rate (what we mean by cache)
Definitions (common cache types we surface):
- Prefix cache hit rate: % of requests where the KV/prefix cache produced a full or partial match that avoided base compute for early tokens.
- Response cache hit rate: % of requests fully served from response cache (rare for generative but common for templated completions or embeddings).
- Embedding cache hit rate: percent of embedding requests returned from a local cache (keyed by text fingerprint).

Calculation guidance:
- Numerator/Denominator: hits / total eligible requests (eligible = requests with a cacheable fingerprint present after normalization). Always surface eligibility rate; low eligibility can make hit-rate meaningless.
- Partial hits: we record partial prefix hits as separate metric (e.g., first 32 tokens hit) — report both full-hit% and partial-hit% and average tokens saved per hit.

QBR framing for cache metrics:
- Show: eligibility %, full-hit %, partial-hit %, avg tokens saved per hit, estimated cost saved.
- Example line: "Embedding cache eligibility 43%, full-hit 67%, estimated monthly saving $1.8k (9.6% of embedding spend)."

5) KPI table for QBR (template)
Header: Metric | Window | Value | Target | Trend | Owner | Action
- Latency (p95 short) | 30d | 185ms | <180ms | up 7% | eng-sre | investigate decode tail
- Latency (p95 medium) | 30d | 340ms | <350ms | down 3% | eng-serving-runtime | keep monitoring
- Availability (API) | 30d | 99.93% | 99.9% | flat | platform-eng | postmortem published
- Cost-per-token (effective) | 30d | $0.00258 | $0.00300 | down 14% | finance-cs | review pricing tier for renewal
- Cache eligibility | 30d | 38% | 45% | up 2% | solutions-eng | canonicalize prompts
- Cache full-hit | 30d | 62% | 65% | down 1% | platform-eng | tune prefix matcher
- Renewal risk score | current | Moderate | Low | up | csm-team | schedule pre-renewal health call

6) Data sources and instrumentation checklist (for CS Ops)
- Ensure QBR numbers come from single canonical sources: usage billing exports, observability (tracing + metrics), and cache telemetry exports. Avoid mixing ad-hoc dashboards.
- Key graphs to attach: latency distribution histograms; stacked p95 contributor bars; rolling availability chart; CPT month-by-month; cache eligibility and hit rate over time.

7) Playbook snippets for CSMs (action-oriented)
- If p95 short > target by >15% for two weeks: propose performance canary (route 5% traffic to tuned variant) + provide customer with ETA for rollback plan.
- If availability < SLA for 30d: offer a root-cause summary w/ mitigation plan and propose a goodwill credit if customer impacted revenue (CSM + Legal).
- If effective CPT improves >10% and customer is near renewal: prepare a pricing brief showing realized efficiency + proposed committed discount to lock-in savings.
- If cache eligibility < 25% and customer expects savings: run a prompt canonicalization audit (Solutions Eng + DevRel) and propose a 6-week remediation.

8) Renewal/Commercial framing language (examples)
- Positive angle: "Your effective cost-per-token decreased 14% YoY largely due to cache and batching improvements — this enables us to discuss an upgraded committed tier that preserves pricing while scaling usage."
- Risk mitigation: "Availability dips in Q4 were addressed; we've applied a regional fallback and propose a targeted SLA amendment for peak windows."

9) Appendix: quick math cheatsheet
- Effective CPT = (Raw platform cost - committed discounts - cache savings estimate) / billable tokens.
- Cache savings estimate = avg tokens saved per cache-hit * CPT * number of hits (adjust for model family multiplier).
- Availability % = 100 * (successful_requests / total_requests_eligible).

Notes to self / meeting prep checklist (CSM)
- Bring 2 slides: 1) top-line KPI table + trend, 2) breakdown of latency contributions and proposed actions.
- Have raw billing export and the last 30d cache telemetry ready for any deep-dive asks.
- Practice the renewal pitch that ties cost-efficiency improvements to a recommended committed tier.
